slos.description:
define ‘chemistry’ and its various branches:
a. analytical chemistry,
b. astrochemistry,
c. biochemistry,
d. environmental chemistry,
e. geochemistry,
f. industrial chemistry,
g. inorganic chemistry,
h. nuclear chemistry,
i. organic chemistry,
j. physical chemistry,
k. polymer chemistry;
explain the significance of the branches of chemistry mentioned in SLO 1.1.1;
describe the contribution of Jabir Ibn Hayyan and Al-Razi in chemistry during the Islamic Golden Age (8th to 14th centuries);
define the term ‘scientific paradigm’;

subtopics.name: 1.3 Basic Definitions, Comparisons, Valencies, and Chemical Formulae

slos.description:
define the following terms:
a. atoms,
b. elements,
c. compounds,
d. mixtures,
e. molecules;

differentiate between:
a. atoms and molecules,
b. atoms and ions,
c. molecules and molecular ions,
d. ions and free radicals;
differentiate among elements, compounds and mixtures;
classify the chemical species into elements, mixtures, compounds, ions, molecular ions and free radicals;
define the term ‘valency’;
determine valencies of common elements and ions (radicals) independently or in compounds;
determine the formula of a compound based on the valencies of elements and ions (radicals).

examSpec.erqGroup: Combined with Topic 5: 6 Marks (Choose any ONE from TWO)

slos.description:
define the following terms:
a. gram atomic mass,
b. gram molecular mass,
c. gram formula mass,
d. formula unit,
e. mole,
f. Avogadro’s number;
relate gram atomic mass, gram molecular mass and gram formula mass to mole and Avogadro’s number;

calculate the following quantities of chemical species:
a. number of moles,
b. number of particles (atoms, molecules and ions),
c. molar mass (atomic/ molecular/ formula),
d. mass;
differentiate between empirical formula and molecular formula;
calculate the percentage composition by mass of an element in a compound;
calculate the empirical formula using percentages or masses of elements;
calculate the molecular formula using molecular mass and empirical formula;

illustrate the following types of chemical reactions:
a. displacement (single/ double),
b. decomposition,
c. addition/ synthesis/ combination,
d. combustion (complete/ incomplete),
e. neutralisation,
f. hydrolysis;

evaluate the effectiveness of chemical reactions based on the following characteristics:
a. change of state,
b. change in colour,
c. evolution of gas,
d. change in temperature,
e. formation of a precipitate,
f. occurrence of sound;
construct chemical equations and ionic equations to show reactants forming products, including state symbols;
balance chemical equations by inspection or trial and error method;

solve problems based on stoichiometric relationships of substances in terms of:
a. mass,
b. number of moles,
c. number of molecules,
d. mole ratio,
e. volume of gases at Room Temperature and Pressure (RTP) (24 L or dm³ and 24000 mL or cm³).
describe the structure of an atom with reference to the location, relative electric charges and relative masses of proton, electron and neutron;

define the following terms:
a. atomic (proton) number,
b. mass (nucleon) number,
c. atomic mass,
d. atomic mass unit;
calculate the atomic number, mass number, number of electrons and neutrons of atoms and ions;
draw the atomic structure of the first twenty elements of the periodic table and their ions (cations and anions) using their mass number and atomic number;

define the following terms:
a. isotopes,
b. average atomic mass,
c. relative atomic mass based on C-12 scale,
d. radioactive isotopes,
e. radioactivity;
determine the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in different isotopes of H, C, O, Cl and U;
calculate the relative atomic masses of chlorine and boron by using the mass number and natural abundance of their isotopes;
explain the role of isotopes in carbon dating (carbon), power generation (uranium) and medical imaging (iodine, sodium, technetium, thallium, arsenic, cobalt and xenon);

subtopics.name: 3.3 Models to Understand the Structure of an Atom

slos.description: explain Rutherford’s experiment leading to the discovery of the atomic nucleus;
explain the defects of Rutherford’s atomic model;
describe the main points (postulates) of Bohr’s atomic model;
differentiate between shells and sub-shells of an atom;
deduce the electronic arrangement (in shells) and electronic configuration (of sub-shells) of the first twenty elements and their ions using their atomic number and charges (if any).
state the modern periodic law;
differentiate between a period and a group in the periodic table;
determine the group, period and block of an element using its electronic configuration (first twenty elements);
describe the demarcation of the periodic table into s, p, d, and f-blocks;
determine the location of families on the periodic table based on their characteristics and electronic configuration (representative elements);

define the following terms:
a. shielding effect,
b. electronegativity,
c. atomic radii,
d. electron affinity,
e. ionisation energy (1st and 2nd);

explain the periodic trend of the following within a group and a period of the periodic table:
a. shielding effect,
b. electronegativity,
c. atomic radii,
d. electron affinity,
e. ionisation energy (1st and 2nd);

compare the chemical reactivity and physical properties (metallic character, physical states, conductivity, density, melting and boiling points) of elements in the same family of elements (representative elements);

subtopics.name: 4.3 Properties of Elements in a Group

slos.description: determine elements as an alkali metal, an alkaline earth metal, a halogen and a noble gas based on their electronic configuration;

compare the general properties of metals and non-metals in terms of:
a. physical states,
b. density,
c. malleability,
d. ductility,
e. melting and boiling points,
f. conductivity,
g. sonority,
h. appearance/ lustre,
i. hardness/ brittleness,
j. nature of oxides (basic, acidic and amphoteric);

explain the following properties of Group I and II elements;
a. occurrence in combined state in nature,
b. softness of metals,
c. reaction with water,
d. reaction with hydrogen,
e. reaction with oxygen,
f. reaction with dilute acids;

explain the following properties of Group VII elements:
a. existence as diatomic molecules,
b. appearance (colour and state),
c. displacement reactions with other halogens,
d. reaction with metals;

explain the following properties of Group VIII elements:
a. existence as monoatomic gases or free state in nature,
b. chemical inertness,
c. importance of noble gas electronic configuration in the formation of ions;

explain the following properties of transition metals:
a. relative hardness,
b. density,
c. melting and boiling points,
d. variable oxidation states,
e. formation of coloured compounds;
explain the inertness of noble metals;
discuss the commercial importance of silver, gold and platinum.

examSpec.erqGroup: Combined with Topic 2: 6 Marks (Choose any ONE from TWO)

slos.description: explain duplet and octet rules that help atoms achieve stable electron configurations by forming bonds;

define a chemical bond and its following types:
a. ionic bond,
b. covalent bond,
c. coordinate covalent bond,
d. metallic bond;
explain the nature of bonding based on the electronegativity difference of bonded atoms using Linus Pauling scale;
explain the formation of an ionic bond;
explain the general characteristics of ionic compounds;
identify a compound as having ionic bond;
draw electron dot and cross structure of a binary ionic compound, for example, NaCl, MgO, K₂O and CaCl₂;
explain the formation of a covalent bond between two non-metallic elements;
exemplify single, double and triple covalent bonds;
explain the general characteristics of covalent compounds;
draw electron dot and cross structures for simple covalent molecules including H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, HCl, CO₂, HCN, C₂H₆, C₂H₄, and C₂H₂;
explain polar and non-polar covalent compounds;
differentiate between ionic and covalent compounds based on characteristics and examples;
explain the formation of coordinate covalent bond;

draw electron dot and cross structure of coordinate covalent compounds, for example, ammonium ion, oxonium (hydronium) ion, aluminium tetrachloride anion, adduct (addition product) of ammonia and boron trifluoride;
compare the formation and characteristics of coordinate covalent compounds with covalent compounds;
explain the formation of metallic bonding (electron-sea model);

explain the contribution of structure of metals and the mobility of their electrons to the following properties:
a. malleability,
b. ductility,
c. melting and boiling points,
d. lustre,
e. tensile strength,
f. electrical and thermal conductivity;

illustrate weak intermolecular forces, including Van der Waals forces (London dispersion forces and dipole-dipole interactions) and hydrogen bonding, and their effects on the melting and boiling points of compounds.

subtopics.name: 6.1 Kinetic Molecular Theory and Phase Changes

slos.description: compare the physical states of matter based on the intermolecular forces present between their molecules;

explain phase changes (melting, freezing, vaporisation, condensation, sublimation and deposition) due to changes in temperature and pressure affecting the arrangement and motion of particles within a substance;
explain melting and boiling point of substances used as a criterion to check their purity;
interpret heating and cooling curves in terms of kinetic theory;

explain the following properties of gases in terms of kinetic theory:
a. diffusion,
b. effusion,
c. density,
d. compressibility;
relate the changes in pressure and volume of a gas using Boyle’s law;
relate the changes in temperature and volume of a gas using Charles’s law;
relate the changes in number of molecules and volume of a gas using Avogadro’s law;

explain the following properties of liquids and the factors that affect them:
a. vapour pressure,
b. boiling point,
c. freezing point,
d. density,
e. compressibility;
differentiate between evaporation and boiling;
discuss the effects of temperature on vapour pressure and the effects of external pressure on the boiling point of liquids;
explain the significance of diffusion rates in the context of medicine;

explain the following physical properties of solids:
a. melting point,
b. density,
c. compressibility;

explain the following applications of sublimation such as:
a. solid air fresheners,
b. dry ice (solid carbon dioxide),
c. mothballs (naphthalene),
d. 3D printing;
define the term ‘allotropes’;
explain allotropic forms of carbon (diamond, graphite, buckyballs and coal) and sulphur (rhombic, monoclinic and plastic).

examSpec.erqGroup: Combined with Topic 8: 6 Marks (Choose any ONE from TWO)

slos.description:
exemplify the following terms:
a. solvent,
b. solute,
c. solution,
d. aqueous/ non-aqueous solution,
e. residue,
f. filtrate;

subtopics.name: 7.2 Types of Solution According to Phases

slos.description:
classify different types of solutions according to the following phases:
a. gas into gas,
b. gas into liquid,
c. gas into solid,
d. liquid into gas,
e. liquid into liquid,
f. liquid into solid,
g. solid into gas,
h. solid into liquid,
i. solid into solid;

subtopics.name: 7.3 Types of Solution According to Concentration

slos.description: differentiate among saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions;
differentiate between dilute and concentrated solutions;

subtopics.name: 7.4 Comparison of Solution, Suspension and Colloid

slos.description: compare the characteristics of solutions, suspensions and colloids with examples;

subtopics.name: 7.5 Concentration Units and Dilution of Solutions

slos.description: define the term ‘molarity’;
solve problems based on molarity of a solution;
define the term ‘percentage’ as a unit of concentration;
calculate the percentage composition of different solutions (% m/m, % m/v, % v/m, % v/v);
solve problems based on dilution of solutions from concentrated solutions of known molarity;
define the term ‘solubility’;
explain the factors that affect solubility, i.e., temperature, pressure and nature of solute and solvent;
predict the solubility of one substance into another using the rule of ‘like dissolves like’;

interpret the effect of temperature on the solubility of different salts (for example, KNO₃, K_Cl, Li₂SO₄, Ce₂(SO₄)₃ and NaCl) in water by referring to absorption, release, or no change in heat, based on the solubility versus temperature graphs;

subtopics.name: 7.7 Methods for Separating Mixtures and Purification Techniques

slos.description:
explain the following methods of separation and purification:
a. evaporation,
b. decantation,
c. filtration,
d. crystallisation,
e. distillation,
f. fractional distillation;

define the following terms:
a. chromatography,
b. stationary phase,
c. mobile phase,
d. chromatogram,
e. locating agent,
f. retention factor (R_f);
apply the paper chromatography technique for separating mixtures and isolating compounds;
interpret chromatograms using the R_f equation and spotting (locating) agents to recognise components in a mixture;
predict techniques for separating and purifying everyday mixtures.

examSpec.erqGroup: Combined with Topic 7: 6 Marks (Choose any ONE from TWO)

slos.description: differentiate between oxidation and reduction in terms of loss or gain of oxygen, hydrogen or electrons;

subtopics.name: 8.2 Oxidation States and Rules for Assigning Oxidation States

slos.description: define oxidation state;
explain the common rules used for assigning oxidation numbers to free elements, ions, molecules and atoms;
calculate the oxidation number of an atom in a compound and polyatomic ion;
describe oxidising and reducing agents in a redox reaction;
deduce oxidising and reducing agents in a redox reaction;

define the following terms:
a. electrolyte,
b. weak electrolyte,
c. non-electrolyte,
d. electrolysis;
describe an electrochemical cell and its two types;
distinguish between Galvanic (voltaic) cell and electrolytic cell based on their parts, working and examples;
deduce the direction of movement of cations and anions towards respective electrodes in an electrolytic cell;
infer the electrical conductivity of solutions based on the dissociation of substances into ions;
identify the reactivity of elements using the reactivity series;
illustrate metal displacement reactions in an aqueous medium;
determine the half-cell in which oxidation occurs and the half-cell in which reduction occurs in a voltaic cell;
deduce the direction of the flow of electrons in a voltaic cell;
explain the production of electrical energy in a dry cell;
explain the manufacturing of sodium metal from fused NaCl in Down cell;
explain the manufacturing of sodium hydroxide from aqueous solution of NaCl in Nelson cell;
define the term ‘corrosion’;
describe the rusting of iron as an example of corrosion;

explain the following methods used to prevent corrosion:
a. barrier coatings (using paint and galvanising),
b. electroplating (using tin and chromium),
c. sacrificial protection (using magnesium blocks).
